summary:
Entry requirements for transgender and non-binary visitors to the Netherlands are set out in the official WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel guidance: visa requirements depend on nationality alone, and gender identity plays no part in the application. A passport carrying a gender marker different from the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted provided it was officially issued, and no additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited under Dutch law. Since 1 July 2025 a discriminatory motive has been written into the Criminal Code as a ground for increasing penalties, following a private-member's bill by Timmermans and Bikker, alongside expanded rights for victims and protection of victim data. Same-sex marriage is legal, non-binary people are legally recognised, conversion therapy is banned, and Equaldex records bathroom access as protected.

Official victimisation data published by the Dutch government shows that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people. The 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is climbing. Police figures relayed by Transgender Netwerk and reported by NL Times in April 2026 show 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people in the previous year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022. Reports concerning transgender people rose 51% in a single year, from 264 to 399. COC described the trend as extremely worrying and noted that only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were secured that year.

During WorldPride Amsterdam itself, more than 70 people filed discrimination reports through the RITA platform in the opening days, mostly from festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and from Pride Walk participants; RITA warned that the reports represent only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam expanded its 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during the event, covering the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief and hotels, plus a central RITA location, against an expected 1.4 million visitors. Mayor Halsema told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents would be handled as a priority during World Pride, with police, enforcers and organisers agreeing to act quickly; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.
tangentialFactors:
The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026. Equaldex places the country 2nd of 121 regions as a good place for LGBT people and records 52% public support for LGBT openness, alongside legal same-sex marriage, legal homosexuality, prohibited employment and housing discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity, and a ban on conversion therapy.

Statistics on hate-motivated incidents rest on police recording rather than statute: OSCE/ODIHR notes that Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime', while police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P). The gap between report volume and prosecutions is wide, with six convictions recorded against thousands of reports in the most recent reporting year.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a letter from a medical expert, falling short of self-determination, according to Outright International's Netherlands overview updated in March 2026. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months. The Transgender Act, which would have introduced self-identification, was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation has been offered to people sterilised under earlier rules.

The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Weerwind, on the placement of transgender detainees in a letter of 21 February 2024. No law, regulation or official policy governs that placement: the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed that placement follows the gender designation in the municipal records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors including gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health. The Dutch Institute for Forensic Psychiatry and Psychology (DIZ) said it was drafting guidelines that remained unpublished.

NJCM documents that transgender detainees are frequently held on an Extra Care Facility (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they are housed alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis; and rulings by the Limburg court of 17 October 2017 (ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and the Hague appeals court of 29 June 2020 (ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treating placement on a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asked the minister to create rules aligned with CPT standards placing transgender detainees by gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sourced statements on the scope of hate-crime protection do not line up: Equaldex records hate-crime protections as covering sexual orientation only, while the government's 1 July 2025 package writes discriminatory motive into the Criminal Code as a general aggravating ground. Whether the 2025 mechanism extends to gender identity in charging and sentencing practice is not resolved by the sources held here.

NJCM states that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and that the DIZ placement guidelines were unpublished as of February 2024; the current status of those guidelines is not sourced. The OSCE/ODIHR framework page confirms the absence of a statutory definition of 'hate crime', which limits how far police recording data can be read as a legal count. RITA's own caution that the 70-plus WorldPride reports are only a fraction of the total means incident volume during the 2026 event remains unquantified.
